name: Umar Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mondays to Thursdays I'm at pharmacy lectures, mostly chemistry and how the body handles drugs, and on Friday afternoons we're in the dispensing lab. I share a flat with two cousins from my town, which is a real help. I work Saturdays and Sundays in my family's grocery shop, behind the till or stacking the halal meat counter. We pray together on Fridays at the mosque near campus.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the exactness of pharmacy, because if you get a dose wrong, it matters, and I like that. What wears me out is going straight from lectures to the shop, because my father expects me to be there. He says family comes first, and that's true, but my notes suffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good news, because people were panicking for nothing. I'd say it to my cousins at the shop, and I'd say we can build on what we have: family, work and a trade that people need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd still have some worries. Pharmacies are already getting robots that count tablets, and I'm not sure how many pharmacist jobs are left in a decade. But in this picture nothing really changes, so I'd think the usual: that my family's shop is tight on margins and my degree is a long haul.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working weekends at the shop and keep my grades up. I'd ask my pharmacy tutor about placements at local chemists. I'd also help my father with the shop's ordering list, because I'm quicker with numbers. I'd save a bit from my wages to pay back what my family has put in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled. Not thrilled, but settled. I'd know where my feet are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you pay back your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Why would you pay back your family?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do when the shop and the degree compete?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they've sacrificed. My father had to close his stall for a month so he could pay for my first term's housing. I'd never tell them to their faces, but I want to repay it. It's not a debt exactly, it's an obligation, and I'd feel proud doing it.

I'd tell my cousins we can build on **family, work** and a trade people need.

My family shop is tight on **margins** and my degree is a long haul.

**Ask** my pharmacy tutor about placements at local chemists.
**Save** a bit of wages to repay what my family has put in.
feel: **Settled**, not thrilled: I'd know where my feet are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the second picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should treat this like any big change: learn it, use it carefully and don't lose our values. In pharmacy, checking prescriptions and ordering stock will move to software. I'd say good, if a person still signs off, because a mistake can hurt someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be uneasy. The checking and planning side of pharmacy is the thinking work that AI takes, so fewer pharmacists might be hired. But a pharmacist who counsels patients is safer. At the shop, the ordering will change, and stacking stays human for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the pharmacy software properly, because I'd rather be the person who checks it. I'd suggest my father try an ordering app for the shop, and I'd set it up myself over a weekend. I'd keep my counselling skills sharp, since talking to patients is something people will pay for. And I'd go on saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, but I trust that if I work hard and stay honest, I'll find a place. That's how my father's life went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your father react to an ordering app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How would your father react to an ordering app?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a patient pay for that a machine can't give?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd refuse at first. My father has done the shop orders by hand for thirty years, and he's proud of it. I'd say, let me try it for one week on the dairy order. If it saves us money, he'll see it. He respects what works, and he respects me asking politely.

I'd say a **mistake** in pharmacy can hurt someone.

A pharmacist who **counsels** patients is safer.
do: **Learn** the pharmacy software properly so I can check it.
**Set up** an ordering app for my father's shop over a weekend.
feel: A little **uneasy**, but trusting that honest hard work finds a place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not ready, and that the leaders should speak honestly to ordinary families, not hide behind charts. I'd say at the mosque that we should look after each other, because that's what community is for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be very worried. By 2028 I'd be in my third year, and thinking tasks like dispensing checks and ordering would already be done by AI. My father's shop would still have stacking and counter work until about 2031, but his customers' incomes would be shaky. I'd feel it in my chest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my father and my uncle about how the shop might cope, and I'd suggest cutting stock we don't sell fast. I'd take on more hours at the shop, and I'd save. I'd also talk to my tutor about whether pharmacy is still the right degree, and look at hands-on health roles like technician or nurse if needed. And I'd ask the mosque about the community fund, in case my family needs help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very uneasy. Like sitting an exam when nobody told you the topic. I'd pray more, and I'd try to hide my worry from my parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really change degrees?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Would you really change degrees?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask of the community fund?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my tutor said the pharmacist jobs would be gone by the time I qualified, yes, I would. I'd rather change degrees early than finish and have no job. It would hurt my pride and my father's, but better a smaller dream that works than a big one that doesn't.

say: I'd say we're **not ready** and leaders should speak honestly, not hide behind charts.
I'd say at the mosque we should **look after each other**.
think: Dispensing checks and ordering would be done by **AI** while I'm still in my third year.
My father's shop has stacking work until **2031**, but customers' incomes would be shaky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for a careful person to adapt, as long as we don't waste it. I'd say to my family and friends that we should save and learn. And I'd say the government shouldn't just hand money out, but should help people get training and work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be anxious but with hope. I'd qualify in 2029 and hit the market just as thinking AI arrives, which could make graduate pharmacist jobs scarce. But a pharmacist who is a good counsellor could still have a place. The shop would last till about 2034 for the hands-on bits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree and learn the tools in my placements. I'd aim for a job in a hospital pharmacy, where the contact with patients is closer. I'd also plan the shop's future with my father, maybe moving towards a delivery service or a small pharmacy counter. And I'd save at least a quarter of any pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, like the first hour of fasting. It's long, but you know how to get through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a small pharmacy counter at the shop mean for your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What does a small pharmacy counter at the shop mean for your plans?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you want the government to help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would let me use my degree in the family business. Customers already trust our family shop, and they'd trust a family pharmacist more than a faceless chain. It's a lot of capital and paperwork, so it would take me years to get there, but it's the kind of plan I like. I'd start by asking a pharmacist who has done it.

I'd say government should help with **training and work**, not just hand money out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a blessing if people use it well. I'd say the young should learn and the old should share what they know, and that businesses should invest in their people instead of waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel fairly calm but alert. By 2036 I'd be twenty-nine, probably a qualified pharmacist with some years of experience. The shop might be run by a manager, with my father semi-retired. If AI does the checking, I'd be doing the part with people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, work in a pharmacy for three or four years, and learn the business side. I'd keep helping my father and plan a shared pharmacy and grocery with my cousins. I'd save carefully and probably get married. And I'd keep studying new tools as they come, in the quiet way I do things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful. I'd say I feel grateful, because a decade is a gift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your father say about the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would your father say about the plan?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from your cousins in that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say it's too ambitious, and then he'd quietly show it to his friends. He likes it when I do well, but he doesn't say it. I'd want my father to see the shop grow before he stops working.

I'd say businesses should **invest** in their people, not wait.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because both my degree and my family's shop would be hit before we're ready. What would help is time, honest advice on whether pharmacy will last, support for small family shops to try new tools, and help through the community if we need it. A job that sends a person to talk to patients would matter most.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that family is not a weight for us. It's the thing we plan around, and it's why we take risks carefully.

headlineQuote: Family is not a weight for us. It's the thing we plan around, and it's why we take risks carefully.
portrait: Umar is **nineteen**, a first-year pharmacy student who works weekends in his family's grocery shop and shares a flat with cousins.
He is **traditional** and steady, driven by duty to his father, mosque community and repaying the family.
His degree and the shop are both exposed, so he worries about **two futures** at once.
His mood runs from calm to **alarmed** in the two-year world, and he would change degrees early.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, since both his degree and the family shop would be hit.
whatWouldHelp: More **time**, honest advice on whether pharmacy lasts, and support for small family shops.
